name: Selma to Montgomery NHT
author: author-D-2026-10-17
summary:
The Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail follows the 54-mile route of the 1965 voting rights marches: from Brown Chapel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Selma, over the Edmund Pettus Bridge and east along U.S. Highway 80 through Dallas and Lowndes counties to the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery. Along the highway, the 2015 foundation document notes, row-crop fields, pastures and woodlots remain largely intact, reflecting the agrarian land use of 1965. Congress established the trail by a law signed on November 12, 1996. [1]

Selma became the focus because of what had been done to its voters. African Americans made up about half of Dallas County’s voting-age population, but since 1901 the county and state had kept them from the polls with literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation; in 1961 only 156 of the county’s 15,000 voting-age African Americans were registered. The 2008 park brochure calls the final march the climactic event of the modern civil rights movement, and the foundation document names the marches an important catalyst for the Voting Rights Act, signed August 6, 1965. [1] [1]

The trail also marks what the right cost. The foundation document records that many suffered from violent opposition and some were murdered, and that after the act passed many Lowndes County tenant farmers were evicted for exercising their right to vote. It defines the trail’s purpose as inspiring all citizens to be vigilant in protecting their constitutional rights. [1]

black.html:
In January 1965 the Southern Christian Leadership Conference joined the Selma campaign. Sheriff Jim Clark directed would-be registrants to an alley, then let no one register; by February 5 more than 3,000 had been arrested. On February 18 in Marion a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson as he tried to defend his grandfather; a call to carry his body to Montgomery became the march. [1] [1]

On March 7 about 600 marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams were tear-gassed and beaten by state troopers and the sheriff’s posse beyond the Edmund Pettus Bridge, opened in 1940 and named, the Historic American Engineering Record notes, for a Confederate general and Alabama senator who also served as a grand dragon in the Alabama Ku Klux Klan. The final march, under federal protection, left Selma on March 21 and reached the Capitol on March 25, some 25,000 strong by the brochure’s count. [1] [1] [1]

women.html: On January 19, 1965, when Amelia Boynton of the Dallas County Voters League was slow to obey Sheriff Clark’s order to move, he grabbed her by the collar and shoved her toward a patrol car; with the photograph of her treatment in major newspapers, the 2008 park brochure says, the media turned its eye on Selma. On the night the march ended, Viola Liuzzo, who had come from Detroit to help, was shot and killed by Klansmen after driving marchers back to Selma; her memorial overlooks the route. The park’s 2015 foundation document warned that Boynton’s Selma home was in disrepair and under threat of demolition. [1] [1]
